source: Kim, Belland, Walker (2018) Effectiveness of computer-based scaffolding in problem-based learning for STEM: Bayesian meta-analysis
finding: Computer-based scaffolding beats no scaffolding in problem-based STEM learning, but the credible interval is wide and effects are small to moderate.
numbers: Overall g = 0.385, 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802 (20,000 MCMC draws). Six moderators, 24 subcategories.
limits: Bayesian priors affect estimates; some subcategories have few studies. Compares scaffold vs no scaffold, not vs direct instruction.
agent_relevance: Scaffolding helps on average but the lower bound is near zero: do not assume benefit without a check.

source: Kim et al. (2018), fading moderator
finding: Scaffolds that both fade and add back (adjust both ways) did best; fade-only and add-only were lower.
limits: Overlapping credible intervals, so the ordering is not firm. Few primary studies fade at all.
agent_relevance: Support-then-withdraw should be two-way: lower help on success, raise it on failure. Fits a program-controlled hint ladder.

source: Kim et al. (2018), customization method moderator
finding: Letting the learner request fading or adding did better than fixed schedules or performance-adapted rules.
numbers: self-selected g = 0.519 (CrI 0.167 to 0.989); fixed time interval g = 0.376; performance-adapted g = 0.434.
limits: Intervals overlap heavily. The paper notes the prior choice shifted estimates (0.162 vs 0.122 for two moderators coded from the same data).
agent_relevance: In an LLM agent the program triggers the fade from its own check results; the evidence does not favour a pure schedule.

source: Kim et al. (2018), scaffold type and skill level
finding: Metacognitive and strategic scaffolds worked best; conceptual scaffolds and question prompts worked least. Higher-order skills like synthesis and evaluation gained little.
numbers: metacognitive g = 0.384; strategic g = 0.345; conceptual g = 0.126; question prompts g = 0.078 (CrI 0.003 to 0.156); synthesis g = 0.156; evaluation g = 0.147; expert modeling g = 0.523; feedback g = 0.474; hints g = 0.375.
limits: Credible intervals wide.
agent_relevance: Generic ask-yourself prompts barely help (matches G1: no doubt on a schedule). Modelled examples and feedback on real output help more (matches G2).

source: Kim et al. (2018), prevalence of fading in the literature
finding: Most scaffolding studies never fade the support, although theory says fading is essential.
numbers: 65% of studies in Belland et al. (2017) had no scaffold customization; Lin et al. (2012) found fading in 9.3% of 43 articles.
limits: Secondary report of other reviews.
agent_relevance: The withdrawal half of support-then-withdraw is rarely tested; our agent has little outside evidence for exact fade rules.

source: Kim et al. (2018), context from other scaffolding and ITS meta-analyses
finding: Reports effect sizes from other reviews: Belland 2017 STEM scaffolding g = 0.46; Kulik and Fletcher 2016 intelligent tutoring g = 0.66; Steenbergen-Hu and Cooper college g = 0.41 and K-12 math g = 0.09; VanLehn 2011 d = 0.76.
limits: Second-hand; the text ties the VanLehn figure to human tutors, which may be a mislabel (check the original).
agent_relevance: Range 0.09 to 0.66 shows large heterogeneity: the effect depends on population and design.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning, Scientific Reports
finding: Crossover RCT in Harvard physics: a structured LLM tutor beat in-class active learning on the post-test.
numbers: N=194; post-test median 4.5 (AI, n=142) vs 3.5 (active learning, n=174); median gains over double; effect size 0.63 (regression), 0.73 to 1.3 SD (quantile regression, ceiling-corrected); median time 49 min vs 60; engagement 4.1 vs 3.6; motivation 3.4 vs 3.1.
limits: Post-test has a ceiling; two short topics; one course; the comparison arm was active learning, not an expert tutor; no delayed test.
agent_relevance: A scaffolded LLM with worked-solution context can match or beat group guided work in the short run.

source: Kestin et al. (2025), design lesson
finding: A system prompt alone could not keep multi-part problems in order, so the platform moved the sequencing into code.
numbers: Authors report the tutor 'would occasionally discuss parts out of sequence'; fix was to guide students sequentially through each part. 83% of students said explanations were accurate.
limits: Authors' observation, not a measured ablation.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the design rule: the program controls step order and the model fills a slot.

source: Kestin et al. (2025), time on task
finding: No correlation between time on the tutor and post-test score.
numbers: 70% of the AI group spent under 60 min; 30% over; median 49 min; no time-score correlation.
limits: Self-paced; confounded by prior knowledge.
agent_relevance: Amount of help-giving time matters less than the structure of the help.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS
finding: Field experiment with nearly 1,000 high-school math students: unguarded GPT-4 help raised practice scores but lowered later unassisted exam scores. A guarded tutor removed the harm but gave no gain.
numbers: Practice: GPT Base +0.137 (+48%), GPT Tutor +0.361 (+127%) over control mean 0.284. Exam (unassisted): GPT Base -0.054 (-17%, p<0.05), GPT Tutor -0.004 (n.s.); control exam mean 0.321, SD 0.277. GPT Base was correct 51% of the time (logic errors 42%, arithmetic 8%).
limits: Three arms assigned by classroom; sessions were about 15% of the semester curriculum; one school system; a PNAS correction was issued and not examined here.
agent_relevance: Help that is never withdrawn becomes a crutch. Practice-with-help scores are not evidence of skill; test unassisted.

source: Bastani et al. (2025), guardrail design
finding: The GPT Tutor arm had teacher-written solutions and prompts that withheld direct answers, which stopped the crutch effect.
numbers: Exam effect -0.004 (SE 0.013) for Tutor vs -0.054 (SE 0.022) for Base.
limits: Cannot separate which guardrail component mattered (hidden answer, hints, step prompts).
agent_relevance: Give the model the verified solution as context and forbid it to hand over the answer.

source: Cohn et al. (2026) Evidence-Decision-Feedback: adaptive scaffolding for LLM agents
finding: A collaborative LLM peer agent in a high-school classroom gave less support as student mastery rose, which is fading seen in logs.
numbers: n=33 dyads (ages 15 to 16); 59% of support requests occurred while mastery was below 40%; requests fell with mastery, Spearman rho = -0.26; grounding 0.43 vs 0.21 baseline, alignment 0.64 vs 0.39, faithfulness 0.48 vs 0.24.
limits: No control group on learning outcomes; small N; modest correlation.
agent_relevance: LLM help can be tied to a mastery estimate and fade, with the program holding the estimate.

source: Cohn et al. (2026), satisfaction cost of withholding
finding: Students liked the inquiry style but were frustrated when the agent withheld direct answers.
numbers: Mean ratings (1 to 5): questions made me think 3.88; questions appropriate 3.81; agent understood me 2.69; suggestions useful 2.77.
limits: Likert surveys, n=33 dyads, no control.
agent_relevance: Withholding has an acceptance cost for human users; for a self-agent the hint ladder still needs a stop rule.

source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2024, v3 2026) Tutor CoPilot
finding: RCT: an LLM that gives live expert-style suggestions to human tutors raised student mastery, most for the weakest tutors.
numbers: 700+ tutors, 1,000+ students; +4 percentage points mastery (p<.01); +9 pp for lower-rated tutors; about $20 per tutor per year; 350,000+ messages show more probing questions and less generic praise.
limits: Math tutoring for underserved students; mastery measured by exit tickets; a human picks the suggestion.
agent_relevance: Guidance modelled on expert reasoning helps the weaker party more than the stronger: an expertise-reversal pattern.

source: Authors (2026) Beyond Access: guided LLM scaffolding in undergraduate statistics
finding: Quasi-experiment: students given an LLM plus training in stepwise help-seeking did better on no-help quizzes than unrestricted-LLM or no-LLM students, but the final exam gap was not significant.
numbers: Start 57, 50 allocated (17 / 17 / 16), 37 analysed (13 / 12 / 12). Quiz 4: Guided beat No-LLM by 23.17 points (g=0.95, p=.022) and Unrestricted by 16.42 (g=0.73, p=.079). Final exam: +14.37 vs No-LLM (g=0.61, p=.127), +14.24 vs Unrestricted (g=0.71, p=.086). Practice scores showed no advantage. Rule compliance 2.43/6 vs 3.21/6 (d=0.81).
limits: Small N, exploratory, 26% attrition, not randomised; authors call results directional.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Bastani at small scale: practice scores mislead, no-help tests show the difference.

source: Zhou et al. (2022) Least-to-most prompting
finding: Breaking a problem into ordered subproblems, easy first, with earlier answers fed forward, lets models solve harder cases than seen in the prompt.
numbers: SCAN length split: 99.7% (code-davinci-002, 14 exemplars) vs 16% chain-of-thought. Last-letter concatenation length 12: 74.0% vs 37.4 to 38.4% CoT. GSM8K overall 62.39% vs 60.97%; problems with 5+ steps 45.23% vs 39.07%.
limits: Task-specific; small gain on GSM8K; needs good decomposition exemplars.
agent_relevance: A machine analogue of scaffolded sequencing. Gain is largest on hard, long problems and near zero on easy ones.

source: Google LearnLM team (2024) Towards responsible development of generative AI for education
finding: Training a model to follow pedagogical system instructions (do not give away the answer, scaffold, ask questions) made expert raters prefer it to leading models.
numbers: Average preference strength 31% over GPT-4o, 11% over Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 13% over Gemini 1.5 Pro; 1,024 explanations in one rater study; simulated learner followed scenario instructions in 93.4% of transcripts.
limits: Expert preference, not learning outcomes; vendor study; used training, not a scaffold alone.
agent_relevance: Default models give away answers; scaffolding behaviour has to be imposed. Our scaffold does it with code gates.

source: Kalyuga and Renkl (2010) Expertise reversal effect, special issue introduction
finding: Guidance that helps novices can hurt people with more knowledge. The effect has been replicated across many materials and often appears as a partial reversal.
numbers: Full reversal (disordinal interaction) or, more often, partial reversal (non-significant difference for one group but a significant interaction). Studied since the mid-1990s.
limits: Intro text; numbers sit in the individual papers. Explanation by cognitive load rests mainly on subjective load ratings.
agent_relevance: Fade the scaffold as checks pass; extra guidance on a solved sub-step is waste and can harm.

source: Kalyuga and Renkl (2010), explanation of the effect
finding: The cognitive-load account: the effect comes from an imbalance between the learner's knowledge and the guidance given. Redundant guidance must be integrated with existing knowledge and costs working memory.
numbers: Not numeric.
limits: Load is inferred, not measured directly in most studies.
agent_relevance: In an LLM, redundant instructions in context may cost similarly; keep guidance minimal once a step is solved.

source: Lazonder and Harmsen (2016) Meta-analysis of inquiry-based learning: effects of guidance, Rev Educ Res
finding: Guidance in inquiry learning helps. Type of guidance matters only for performance success.
numbers: 72 studies; learning activities d=0.66 (CI 0.44 to 0.88); performance success d=0.71 (0.52 to 0.90); learning outcomes d=0.50 (0.37 to 0.62). Too few studies to settle age effects.
limits: Abstract only; full PDF blocked (HTTP 403).
agent_relevance: Benchmark: guided inquiry about d=0.5 over unguided inquiry. Rebuts minimal guidance as a default.

source: Alfieri, Brooks, Aldrich, Tenenbaum (2011) Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning? J Educ Psychol
finding: Unassisted discovery is worse than explicit instruction; assisted discovery is better.
numbers: From memory, unverified: 164 studies; unassisted discovery vs explicit instruction about g = -0.38; assisted discovery vs other forms about g = +0.30.
limits: Not opened; the PDF host returned the wrong file. Verify numbers before citing.
agent_relevance: Core evidence that guided discovery beats both poles.

source: Kirschner, Sweller, Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work, Educ Psychologist
finding: Argues minimal-guidance methods fail for novices because they overload working memory, citing worked-example and direct-instruction advantages.
numbers: From memory: no new data.
limits: Not opened (host unreachable). A position paper, not a meta-analysis; it lumps guided problem-based learning with minimal guidance (see Hmelo-Silver 2007).
agent_relevance: The support half of the schema; pair with expertise reversal for the withdrawal half.

source: Hmelo-Silver, Duncan, Chinn (2007) Scaffolding and achievement in problem-based and inquiry learning, Educ Psychologist
finding: Reply to Kirschner et al.: problem-based and inquiry learning are heavily scaffolded, so they are not minimal guidance; cites positive results.
numbers: From memory: no single effect figure.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Frames the real contrast as scaffolded vs unscaffolded, not discovery vs instruction.

source: Mayer (2004) Should there be a three-strikes rule against pure discovery learning? Am Psychol
finding: Argues three waves of pure discovery (1960s, 1970s to 80s, 1990s) failed; guided discovery works better.
numbers: From memory: no pooled statistic.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Historical pattern of failed unguided methods.

source: Klahr and Nigam (2004) The equivalence of learning paths in early science instruction, Psychol Sci
finding: Control-of-variables strategy: direct instruction produced far more learners who mastered it than discovery; those in the discovery group who did master it transferred as well.
numbers: From memory, unverified: about 112 children, grades 3 and 4; roughly 77% of direct-instruction vs 23% of discovery children mastered the strategy.
limits: Not opened. Narrow strategy; other domains mixed.
agent_relevance: Direct support is efficient; the value of discovery, if any, shows in what masters then transfer.

source: Wood, Bruner, Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving, J Child Psychol Psychiatry
finding: Founding paper: a tutor works with children on a block-construction task; defines scaffolding by six tutor functions; help is contingent on child performance.
numbers: From memory: 30 children aged 3, 4 and 5; six functions (recruitment, reduction of degrees of freedom, direction maintenance, marking critical features, frustration control, demonstration). Qualitative.
limits: Not opened; descriptive, small N, one task. Later reviews show fading is seldom tested.
agent_relevance: Source of the reduce-degrees-of-freedom and mark-critical-features ideas usable as operators.

source: van de Pol, Volman, Beishuizen (2010) Scaffolding in teacher-student interaction, Educ Psychol Rev
finding: Review: contingency, fading and transfer of responsibility are the defining traits of scaffolding; fading is seldom shown.
numbers: From memory: no pooled statistic.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Three traits to check in our own design: contingency, fading, transfer.

source: Koedinger and Aleven (2007) Exploring the assistance dilemma, Educ Psychol Rev
finding: The assistance dilemma: when to give help and when to withhold it; no single level is best and the best depends on knowledge component and learner.
numbers: From memory: no pooled statistic.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat help level as a tuning parameter and test per task.

source: Zosh et al. (2022) Guided play vs direct instruction vs free play, Child Development
finding: Guided play beat direct instruction on some skills and free play on one; no difference on most outcomes.
numbers: 17 studies, total N=3,893 (ages 1 to 8). Guided vs direct: early maths g=0.24, shape knowledge g=0.63, task switching g=0.40. Vs free play: spatial vocabulary g=0.93.
limits: Abstract only via Crossref; guided play defined differently across studies.
agent_relevance: Guided does not broadly beat direct instruction; avoid claiming general superiority.
